questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: What does the rule of law mean in the UK?
options: Only citizens have to obey the law
The police decide what the law is
Religious leaders can set aside the law
Everyone, including the government, must obey the law
questions.explain: The rule of law means that no person or body is above the law. Ministers, officials, the police and ordinary residents are all bound by the same laws, and those laws are applied fairly by independent courts.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which description best fits democracy as a principle of British life?
options: The largest company in each region governs
Only landowners take part in decisions
People choose their representatives in free and fair elections
questions.explain: In a democracy, power rests with the people. Adults who are eligible to vote choose the members of parliaments and councils in free elections, and those representatives must answer to voters at the next election.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which principle means that people are free to make their own choices about their lives, as long as they stay within the law?
questions.explain: Individual liberty is one of the fundamental principles of British life. Adults can decide for themselves how to live, what to believe and what to say, provided they respect the law and the rights of other people.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which principle asks people to accept and respect those whose religion or beliefs differ from their own?
options: Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs
questions.explain: Tolerance of people with different faiths and beliefs is a core British value. People of all religions and of none live side by side in the UK and are expected to respect one another, even when they disagree.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Taking an active part in your neighbourhood, for example through local groups or helping at events, reflects which principle?
questions.explain: Participation in community life is one of the fundamental principles expected of people who settle in the UK. Joining local groups, helping neighbours and getting involved in local decisions all help communities to thrive.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: If you wish to live permanently in the UK, which of these responsibilities are you expected to accept?
options: To attend a place of worship
To live in the same town for life
To respect and obey the law
questions.explain: Anyone who wants to settle permanently in the UK is expected to respect and obey the law. Other responsibilities include respecting the rights of others, treating people fairly and looking after yourself, your family and your area.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Your neighbour holds political opinions that you strongly disagree with. What does respect for the rights of others mean here?
options: Accepting their right to hold and express those opinions lawfully
questions.explain: Respecting the rights of others includes accepting that people may hold opinions different from yours. In the UK, people can express their views freely within the law, and disagreement should be handled through discussion, not hostility.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which of these is a responsibility that comes with living in the UK?
questions.explain: Treating other people fairly, whatever their background, is one of the responsibilities expected of residents. It sits alongside obeying the law, respecting others' rights and looking after yourself, your family and the place where you live.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which responsibility is about supporting your own household where you are able to?
options: Looking after yourself and your family
Asking the state to provide for everything
questions.explain: People living in the UK are expected, where they can, to look after themselves and their families, for example by working and managing their own needs. Support from the state exists for those who are unable to do so.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Not dropping litter and keeping your street tidy are examples of which responsibility?
options: Looking after the area you live in and the environment
questions.explain: Residents are expected to look after the area where they live and the wider environment. Simple actions such as disposing of rubbish properly, recycling and respecting shared spaces are part of being a good neighbour.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Is this statement TRUE or FALSE? In the UK, people are free to follow any religion, to change their religion or to have no religion.
questions.explain: Freedom of belief and religion is protected in the UK. People may practise any faith, convert to another or follow none, and they should not be treated unfairly by the law or by employers because of their choice.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which of these is NOT protected by freedom of speech in the UK?
options: Writing a letter to a newspaper
Encouraging people to commit violence against others
questions.explain: People in the UK can express opinions freely, including strong criticism of the government. Freedom of speech has limits, however: stirring up violence or hatred against others and threatening people are against the law.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: An employer refuses to interview a candidate only because of the candidate's ethnic background. How is this treated in the UK?
options: It is acceptable for small firms
It is allowed if the employer is honest about it
It is a matter of personal choice
questions.explain: Freedom from unfair discrimination is a basic right in the UK. Treating someone less favourably at work because of race, ethnic origin, religion, sex, disability and other protected characteristics is against the law.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: If a person in the UK is accused of a crime, what right do they have?
options: The right to choose the judge
The right to a fair trial
The right to avoid any trial
The right to be tried by their family
questions.explain: Everyone accused of a crime in the UK has the right to a fair trial before an independent court. They are presumed innocent until proven guilty and can have legal representation to present their case.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which freedom allows people in the UK to join with others to protest peacefully against a decision?
questions.explain: People in the UK may gather together and protest peacefully, for example by marching or holding a demonstration. Protests must stay within the law, so violence, damage to property and some kinds of disruption can lead to arrest.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: How many questions are there in the Life in the UK test?
questions.explain: The Life in the UK test contains 24 multiple-choice questions about British traditions, customs, history and institutions. The questions are based only on the official handbook, Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: How long do candidates have to complete the Life in the UK test?
questions.explain: Candidates have 45 minutes to answer the 24 questions of the Life in the UK test. That is just under two minutes per question, which is usually plenty of time for someone who has studied the official handbook well.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: What score do you need to pass the Life in the UK test?
questions.explain: To pass the Life in the UK test you must reach 75 per cent, which means answering at least 18 of the 24 questions correctly. The result is given at the test centre or through the candidate's online account.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Where can the Life in the UK test be taken?
options: At any public library without booking
Only at an approved test centre
questions.explain: The Life in the UK test must be booked online through the official service and taken in person at an approved test centre. Candidates bring identification, and tests taken anywhere else are not accepted for immigration purposes.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which official book are the Life in the UK test questions based on?
options: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents
A History of the English-Speaking Peoples
questions.explain: All the questions in the test come from the official handbook Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, published for the Home Office. The current edition is the third, and candidates are only tested on its content.

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which group does NOT normally need to take the Life in the UK test when applying for settlement or citizenship?
options: People who have lived in London
questions.explain: Applicants under 18 and those aged 65 or over do not normally need to pass the Life in the UK test. Some people with a long-term physical or mental condition can also be exempted on medical evidence.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Is this statement TRUE or FALSE? If you fail the Life in the UK test, you are not allowed to take it again.
questions.explain: The statement is false. A candidate who fails the Life in the UK test can rebook it as many times as needed. Each attempt has to be booked and paid for again, so careful study of the handbook before the first attempt saves time and money.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Alongside the Life in the UK test, applicants usually have to show English speaking and listening skills at which minimum level?
options: A1 on the Common European Framework of Reference
B1 on the Common European Framework of Reference
C2 on the Common European Framework of Reference
questions.explain: Most applicants for settlement or citizenship must prove they can speak and listen in English at level B1 or above of the Common European Framework of Reference, or hold a degree taught in English, unless an exemption applies.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Passing the Life in the UK test is one of the requirements for which applications?
options: Settlement (indefinite leave to remain) and British citizenship
questions.explain: The Life in the UK test is required for most people applying for indefinite leave to remain, also called settlement, and for those applying to become British citizens by naturalisation. It is not needed for short-term visas.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: At a citizenship ceremony, what can a person who does not wish to swear by God do instead of taking the oath?
options: Sign a contract with the council
questions.explain: New citizens make either an oath of allegiance, which refers to God, or an affirmation, which has the same legal effect without religious words. Everyone then makes the citizenship pledge to the United Kingdom.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Who organises citizenship ceremonies for new British citizens?
questions.explain: Citizenship ceremonies are organised by local authorities. Successful applicants receive an invitation from the Home Office and then arrange their ceremony, which must normally take place within three months of the invitation.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Within what period must you normally attend your citizenship ceremony after receiving your invitation from the Home Office?
questions.explain: Applicants approved for British citizenship must normally attend a ceremony within three months of receiving their invitation from the Home Office. A person only becomes a citizen once they have made the oath or affirmation and the pledge.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: What do new citizens receive at the end of their citizenship ceremony?
questions.explain: At the end of the ceremony new citizens are given their certificate of British citizenship and usually a welcome pack. A British passport is not issued at the ceremony; it must be applied for separately afterwards.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: In the citizenship pledge, what do new citizens promise to do with the laws of the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: The citizenship pledge is a promise of loyalty to the United Kingdom. New citizens commit to respecting its rights and freedoms, upholding its democratic values, observing its laws faithfully and fulfilling their duties as citizens.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Does UK law require you to give up your other nationality when you become a British citizen?
options: No, UK law allows dual nationality
Yes, unless you marry a British citizen
Only if you were born in Europe
questions.explain: The United Kingdom allows its citizens to hold another nationality at the same time. Whether you can keep your original nationality depends on the law of that other country, so applicants should check its rules.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which UK law made the rights in the European Convention on Human Rights directly enforceable in UK courts?
questions.explain: The Human Rights Act 1998 brought the rights of the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law. People can rely on rights such as the right to life, liberty and a fair trial directly in courts in the UK.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which Act brought together laws protecting people in England, Scotland and Wales from discrimination at work and in services?
questions.explain: The Equality Act 2010 combined earlier anti-discrimination laws for Great Britain into one Act. It protects people from unfair treatment because of characteristics such as age, disability, race, religion, sex and sexual orientation.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Is this statement TRUE or FALSE? In the UK, it is a criminal offence to force someone to marry against their will.
questions.explain: Marriage in the UK must be entered into freely by both people. Forcing someone to marry, including taking them abroad for that purpose, is a criminal offence, and courts can also issue orders to protect people at risk.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: How does UK law treat violence by one partner against the other within a marriage or relationship?
options: It is a private family matter
It is allowed if no one is injured
It is only a crime outside the home
It is a crime, whether or not the couple are married
questions.explain: Domestic abuse is a serious crime in the UK. Violence, threats and controlling behaviour against a partner are illegal, including within marriage, and anyone at risk can seek help from the police or specialist support services.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: What is the legal position of female genital mutilation (FGM) in the UK?
options: It is illegal, including arranging for it to be done abroad
It is legal with parental consent
It is legal if done by a doctor
It is only illegal for adults
questions.explain: Female genital mutilation is a crime in the UK. It is also an offence to take a girl abroad for FGM or to help arrange it, and those found guilty can face a long prison sentence.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which of these rights do women in the UK have on the same terms as men?
options: The right to work, own property and vote
Only the right to own property
None, these depend on their husband
questions.explain: Women and men in the UK have equal rights in law. Women can work, own and inherit property, vote and stand for election, and it is unlawful to pay them less than men for doing the same or equivalent work.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Can newspapers in the UK publish articles criticising the government?
options: No, the government must approve every article
Yes, the UK has a free press
questions.explain: The UK has a free press, so newspapers, broadcasters and websites can report on and criticise the government. Like everyone else, the media must still obey the law, for example on defamation and contempt of court.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: What is permanent residence in the UK commonly called in official language?
options: Leave to enter for six months
questions.explain: Settlement in the UK is officially called indefinite leave to remain. It allows a person to live, work and study in the UK without time limits, and it is usually a step towards applying for British citizenship.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Who is expected to share the fundamental principles of British life?
options: Only people born in the UK
Only members of the armed forces
Only people who own a home
Everyone who lives in the UK, whatever their background
questions.explain: The fundamental principles of British life, such as democracy, the rule of law and tolerance, are shared values for all residents. They apply equally to people born in the UK and to those who have come to settle.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The values and principles of the UK

questions.chapter: The values and principles of the UK
questions.q: Which of these is a freedom that people in the UK can enjoy under the rules of democracy?
options: Taking part in the election of a government
questions.explain: One of the freedoms of life in the UK is the right of eligible citizens to take part in choosing a government through free elections. Voting is by secret ballot, so nobody can force a person to vote a certain way.
