questions.q: What is the capital city of Wales?
questions.explain: Cardiff is the capital city of Wales. It is the largest Welsh city and the home of the Senedd (Welsh Parliament), which makes laws for Wales on many devolved matters such as health and education.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the name of the national flag of the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: The national flag of the UK is the Union Flag, often called the Union Jack. It combines the cross of St George for England, the cross of St Andrew for Scotland and the cross of St Patrick for Ireland.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which four countries make up the United Kingdom?
options: England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland
England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
England, Wales, Ireland and the Isle of Man
England, Scotland, Jersey and Northern Ireland
questions.explain: The United Kingdom is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. The rest of the island of Ireland is the Republic of Ireland, an independent country that is not part of the UK.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which country is part of the UK but NOT part of Great Britain?
questions.explain: Great Britain is the name for England, Scotland and Wales together, which share the largest island. The United Kingdom adds Northern Ireland, which lies on the island of Ireland, to form the full country.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the full official name of the country?
options: The Kingdom of England and Ireland
The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
questions.explain: The official name is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. It is usually shortened to the United Kingdom or the UK, and the word Britain is often used in everyday speech to mean the whole country.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the status of the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man?
options: Crown dependencies, closely linked to the UK but not part of it
questions.explain: The Channel Islands and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies. They have their own governments and laws, but the UK is responsible for their defence and international relations. They are not part of the United Kingdom.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which of these is a British overseas territory?
questions.explain: The UK has several overseas territories around the world, including the Falkland Islands, Gibraltar and Bermuda. They are linked to the UK but are not part of it, and they differ from the Crown dependencies near Britain.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the capital city of Scotland?
questions.explain: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland and the seat of the Scottish Parliament at Holyrood. Glasgow is Scotland's largest city, but it has never been the capital, which is a common source of confusion.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the capital city of Northern Ireland?
questions.explain: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland and the home of the Northern Ireland Assembly at Stormont. Dublin is the capital of the Republic of Ireland, a separate country that is not part of the UK.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Why does the Union Flag not include a symbol for Wales?
options: Wales was already united with England when the first Union Flag was created
Wales asked to be left out
Wales has never been part of the UK
The Welsh dragon was removed in 1997
questions.explain: The first Union Flag of 1606 combined the crosses of England and Scotland. Wales had already been united with England for many years, so it was not separately represented, and the Welsh dragon appears instead on the flag of Wales.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: How is the cross of St George, patron saint of England, shown?
options: A white diagonal cross on a blue background
A red cross on a white background
A red diagonal cross on a white background
A yellow cross on a green background
questions.explain: The flag of St George is a red upright cross on a white field. It is used as the flag of England and forms the central red cross of the Union Flag, which combines it with the crosses of St Andrew and St Patrick.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: How is the cross of St Andrew, patron saint of Scotland, shown?
options: A red cross on a white background
A red diagonal cross on a white background
A white diagonal cross on a blue background
A green cross on a white background
questions.explain: The cross of St Andrew, also called the Saltire, is a white diagonal cross on a blue background. It is the national flag of Scotland and provides the blue field and white diagonals of the Union Flag.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: How is the cross of St Patrick shown on the Union Flag?
options: A white diagonal cross on a blue background
A red diagonal cross on a white background
questions.explain: The cross of St Patrick is a red diagonal cross on a white background. It was added to the Union Flag in 1801, when Great Britain and Ireland were united, and represents Ireland in the flag.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What appears on the national flag of Wales?
options: A red dragon on a green and white background
questions.explain: The flag of Wales shows a red dragon on a background of white and green. Because Wales is not represented in the Union Flag, the Welsh dragon is a strong and widely used symbol of Welsh identity.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In which year did the Union Flag take the form used today, with the cross of St Patrick added?
questions.explain: The present Union Flag dates from 1801, when the Act of Union with Ireland came into force and the cross of St Patrick was added to the crosses of St George and St Andrew already used since the early 1600s.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Apart from English, which language is widely spoken and taught in schools in Wales?
questions.explain: Welsh is an official language in Wales and is spoken by a large part of the population. It is taught in schools, and public signs and many official documents in Wales appear in both Welsh and English.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In which part of the UK is Scottish Gaelic mainly spoken?
options: The Highlands and Islands of Scotland
questions.explain: Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language spoken mainly in parts of the Highlands and the Western Isles of Scotland. It is recognised as an official language of Scotland and there are Gaelic-medium schools and broadcasting.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which is the longest river in the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: The River Severn is the longest river in the UK. It rises in the Welsh mountains and flows through Wales and England into the Bristol Channel. The River Thames, which runs through London, is the second longest.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain in the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: Ben Nevis, near Fort William in the Scottish Highlands, is the highest mountain in the UK at about 1,345 metres. It attracts large numbers of walkers and climbers every year.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the highest mountain in Wales?
questions.explain: Yr Wyddfa, also known in English as Snowdon, is the highest mountain in Wales. It stands in the Eryri (Snowdonia) National Park in north-west Wales and can be reached on foot or by a mountain railway.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which is the highest mountain in England?
questions.explain: Scafell Pike, in the Lake District in Cumbria, is the highest mountain in England at about 978 metres. Ben Nevis in Scotland and Yr Wyddfa in Wales are the highest peaks in their own countries.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which is the largest lake in the United Kingdom by surface area?
questions.explain: Lough Neagh in Northern Ireland is the largest lake in the UK by surface area. Loch Ness in Scotland is famous for its depth and legends, and Windermere is the largest natural lake in England.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In which part of England is the Lake District national park?
questions.explain: The Lake District is in Cumbria, in the north-west of England. Known for its lakes, mountains and literary history, it is a World Heritage Site and one of the most visited national parks in the UK.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Where is the Giant's Causeway, a coastline of thousands of basalt columns?
questions.explain: The Giant's Causeway lies on the north coast of County Antrim in Northern Ireland. Its thousands of interlocking basalt columns were formed by ancient volcanic activity, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In which English county is Stonehenge, the prehistoric stone circle?
questions.explain: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, in the south of England. It was built in stages during the Stone Age and Bronze Age and is one of the most famous prehistoric monuments in the world.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: The Eden Project, with its giant greenhouses holding plants from around the world, is in which county?
questions.explain: The Eden Project is near St Austell in Cornwall, in the far south-west of England. Its large domes, called biomes, house plants from rainforest and Mediterranean climates and it is a popular educational attraction.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is 'Big Ben'?
options: The great bell of the clock at the Palace of Westminster
questions.explain: Big Ben is the nickname of the great bell in the clock tower of the Palace of Westminster, where Parliament sits. The tower itself was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012, but many people still call the whole structure Big Ben.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Where in London are the Crown Jewels kept?
questions.explain: The Crown Jewels are displayed at the Tower of London, a fortress beside the Thames begun by William the Conqueror. Over the centuries the Tower has been a royal palace, a prison and a place of execution.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which is the largest national park in the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: The Cairngorms National Park in the Scottish Highlands is the largest national park in the UK. It includes mountains, forests and rivers and is home to rare wildlife such as the capercaillie and the red squirrel.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the currency of the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: The currency of the UK is the pound sterling, divided into 100 pence. Shillings were used before decimal currency was introduced in 1971, and the euro is used in many European Union countries but not in the UK.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Banks in which parts of the UK issue their own banknotes?
options: The Isle of Wight and Kent
questions.explain: Several banks in Scotland and Northern Ireland issue their own banknotes in pounds. These notes can be used throughout the UK, although shops elsewhere are not obliged to accept them. In England and Wales, notes come from the Bank of England.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a coin in everyday use in the UK?
questions.explain: UK coins in everyday use are 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2. There is no 25p coin in general circulation, although special 25p crowns have occasionally been minted to mark royal events.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which flower is the national emblem of Scotland?
questions.explain: The thistle is the national flower of Scotland. Legend says that a barefoot invader stepped on a thistle and cried out, warning the Scots of an attack. It appears on many Scottish badges and coats of arms.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which flower is the national emblem of Wales?
questions.explain: The daffodil is the national flower of Wales, and the leek is also a traditional Welsh emblem. Many people in Wales wear a daffodil or a leek on 1 March to celebrate St David's Day.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which plant is the traditional emblem of Northern Ireland and of Ireland as a whole?
questions.explain: The shamrock, a small three-leaved clover, is the traditional emblem of Ireland. According to tradition, St Patrick used it to explain the Christian Trinity, and it is widely worn on St Patrick's Day.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which flower is the national emblem of England?
questions.explain: The rose is the national flower of England. It dates back to the Wars of the Roses, after which the Tudor rose combined the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York into a single royal badge.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which country is linked to England by the Channel Tunnel?
questions.explain: The Channel Tunnel runs under the English Channel between Kent in England and the Pas-de-Calais in France. It opened in 1994 and carries passenger trains and vehicle shuttles between the two countries.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which sea lies between Great Britain and the island of Ireland?
questions.explain: The Irish Sea separates Great Britain from the island of Ireland. Ferry routes cross it between ports such as Holyhead, Liverpool and Cairnryan on one side and Dublin and Belfast on the other.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: With which country does the UK share a land border?
questions.explain: The only land border of the United Kingdom is between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, on the island of Ireland. The UK is otherwise surrounded by sea, with France reached by tunnel or ferry.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: The Orkney and Shetland islands are part of which country of the UK?
questions.explain: Orkney and Shetland are groups of islands off the far north coast of mainland Scotland and are part of Scotland. They have a strong Norse heritage, having been ruled by Norway until the fifteenth century.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In which year was the Magna Carta agreed by King John?
questions.explain: King John agreed to the Magna Carta in 1215 after pressure from his barons. It limited the power of the monarch, who had to respect the law like everyone else, and it is seen as one of the founding texts of the rule of law in England.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which battle in 1066 led to the Norman conquest of England?
questions.explain: At the Battle of Hastings in 1066, William, Duke of Normandy, defeated the English King Harold, who was killed in the fighting. William was crowned king and Norman rule brought big changes to government, language and land ownership in England.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who wrote the plays Romeo and Juliet and Hamlet?
questions.explain: William Shakespeare, born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, wrote both plays as well as many other tragedies, comedies and sonnets. He is widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language and his works are still performed around the world.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Skara Brae, one of the best-preserved prehistoric villages in northern Europe, is in which place?
questions.explain: Skara Brae is a Stone Age village on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland. Its stone houses, with built-in furniture, were uncovered by a storm in the nineteenth century and give a rare view of life over 5,000 years ago.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In which year did the Roman invasion of Britain begin under Emperor Claudius?
questions.explain: Julius Caesar landed in Britain in 55 BC but did not stay. The real Roman conquest began in AD 43 under Emperor Claudius, and much of Britain remained part of the Roman Empire for nearly 400 years.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who was Boudicca?
options: The first Roman governor of Britain
A Viking queen who settled in York
The queen of the Iceni who led a revolt against the Romans
questions.explain: Boudicca was queen of the Iceni tribe in what is now East Anglia. Around AD 60 she led a major uprising against Roman rule and her forces burned several towns before being defeated. A statue of her stands near Parliament in London.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Why did the Romans build Hadrian's Wall in the north of England?
options: To mark the northern frontier and keep out the Picts
questions.explain: Emperor Hadrian ordered the wall to be built across northern England in the AD 120s to guard the frontier of Roman Britain against tribes to the north, including the Picts. Parts of it can still be walked today.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which peoples invaded and settled much of Britain after the Romans left?
questions.explain: After the Roman army left in the early fifth century, tribes from northern Europe, the Angles, Saxons and Jutes, settled across much of what became England. Their kingdoms and language laid the foundations of English.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who was sent by the Pope in AD 597 and became the first Archbishop of Canterbury?
questions.explain: In AD 597 Pope Gregory sent St Augustine to spread Christianity among the Anglo-Saxons in the south of England. He converted the king of Kent and became the first Archbishop of Canterbury, still the senior bishop of the Church of England.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What was found at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk?
options: The burial ship of an Anglo-Saxon king
questions.explain: At Sutton Hoo in Suffolk, archaeologists found the buried remains of a large ship filled with treasures and weapons. It is thought to be the grave of an Anglo-Saxon king, probably buried in the early seventh century.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: From which countries did the Vikings who raided Britain mainly come?
questions.explain: The Vikings came mainly from Denmark and Norway. They began raiding the coasts of Britain in the late eighth century, and many later settled, especially in the east and north of England and in parts of Scotland.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which Anglo-Saxon king of Wessex is famous for defeating the Vikings in the ninth century?
questions.explain: Alfred the Great, king of Wessex, united Anglo-Saxon forces and defeated the Vikings at the Battle of Edington in 878. He also built fortified towns and encouraged learning, and later generations gave him the title 'the Great'.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What does the Bayeux Tapestry show?
options: The events of the Norman conquest of England
questions.explain: The Bayeux Tapestry is a long embroidered cloth that tells the story of the Norman conquest of England, including the Battle of Hastings in 1066. It is kept in Bayeux, in Normandy, France.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What was the Domesday Book?
options: A survey of land, people and property ordered by William the Conqueror
questions.explain: William the Conqueror ordered the Domesday Book, completed in 1086, to record who owned land in England and what it was worth. It listed towns, villages, people and even animals, and it still survives today.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who led the Scots to victory over the English at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314?
questions.explain: Robert the Bruce, king of Scotland, defeated the army of Edward II at Bannockburn in 1314. The victory was a turning point in the wars of Scottish independence and Scotland remained unconquered by England.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which English king won the Battle of Agincourt in France in 1415?
questions.explain: Henry V led a heavily outnumbered English army to victory over the French at Agincourt in 1415, during the Hundred Years War. The battle became famous partly through Shakespeare's play Henry V.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What was the Black Death that reached England in 1348?
options: A plague that killed a large part of the population
questions.explain: The Black Death was a deadly plague that swept across Europe and reached England in 1348. It killed a large share of the population, perhaps a third or more, and the resulting shortage of workers changed farming and society.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who wrote The Canterbury Tales, stories told by pilgrims travelling to Canterbury?
questions.explain: Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in the late fourteenth century. Written in Middle English, the poems describe pilgrims of many backgrounds telling stories on their way to Canterbury and are among the earliest great works of English literature.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who set up the first printing press in England in the 1470s?
questions.explain: William Caxton brought printing to England and set up his press at Westminster in the 1470s. One of the first books he printed was The Canterbury Tales, and printing helped spread books and ideas far more widely.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which two royal houses fought each other in the Wars of the Roses?
options: The House of Tudor and the House of Stuart
The House of Lancaster and the House of York
The House of Windsor and the House of Hanover
The House of Normandy and the House of Wessex
questions.explain: The Wars of the Roses were fought in the fifteenth century between the House of Lancaster, whose symbol was a red rose, and the House of York, with a white rose. They ended when Henry Tudor won the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Why did Henry VIII break away from the Roman Catholic Church?
options: He wanted to move the capital to York
The Pope tried to invade England
The Pope refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon
questions.explain: When the Pope refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, Henry VIII broke with Rome and made himself head of the Church in England. This led to the creation of the Church of England, independent of the Pope.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In 1588, during the reign of Elizabeth I, which fleet did the English defeat?
questions.explain: In 1588 the Spanish Armada, a large fleet sent by Philip II of Spain to invade England, was defeated by the English navy and damaged by storms. The victory became one of the best-remembered events of Elizabeth I's reign.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who was the first Englishman to sail all the way around the world?
questions.explain: Sir Francis Drake sailed around the world between 1577 and 1580 in his ship, the Golden Hind. He was one of the leading commanders who later fought against the Spanish Armada in 1588.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What happened in 1603 when Elizabeth I died without children?
options: James VI of Scotland also became James I of England
questions.explain: When Elizabeth I died in 1603, her cousin James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne and became James I of England. The two countries then shared a monarch, although they kept separate parliaments for another century.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which Act of 1707 joined England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain?
questions.explain: The Act of Union of 1707 united the kingdoms of England and Scotland to form the Kingdom of Great Britain with one parliament at Westminster. Scotland kept its own legal system, education system and Presbyterian church.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who led the parliamentary side in the English Civil War and later became Lord Protector?
questions.explain: Oliver Cromwell was a leading commander of the parliamentary army in the Civil War against Charles I. After the king was executed in 1649, England became a republic and Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector until his death in 1658.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In which year did the Great Fire destroy much of the city of London?
questions.explain: In September 1666 a fire that started in a bakery in Pudding Lane spread across the City of London for several days. It destroyed thousands of houses and many churches, including the old St Paul's Cathedral.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which architect designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of London?
questions.explain: Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral, with its famous dome, and many other churches rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1666. He is buried in the cathedral he created.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who was invited to take the English throne in 1688, in what became known as the Glorious Revolution?
questions.explain: In 1688 leading English politicians invited the Protestant William of Orange, ruler of the Netherlands, to take the throne from the Catholic James II. William and his wife Mary became joint monarchs, and Parliament's power grew.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Whose improvements to the steam engine helped drive the Industrial Revolution?
questions.explain: The Scottish engineer James Watt greatly improved the efficiency of the steam engine in the eighteenth century. His engines powered factories, mines and mills and helped make Britain the first industrialised country.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which Member of Parliament is best known for leading the campaign to end the British slave trade?
questions.explain: William Wilberforce, an MP from Yorkshire, campaigned for years against the trade in enslaved people. Parliament abolished the slave trade in the British Empire in 1807, and slavery itself was abolished across the empire by an Act of 1833.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which admiral was killed at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 and is remembered by a column in London?
questions.explain: Admiral Nelson led the British fleet to victory over the French and Spanish at Trafalgar in 1805 but was killed during the battle. Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square, London, was built in his memory.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who commanded the British army that defeated Napoleon at Waterloo in 1815?
questions.explain: The Duke of Wellington, with allied forces, defeated Napoleon at Waterloo, in present-day Belgium, in 1815. This ended the Napoleonic Wars. Wellington later became Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Florence Nightingale became famous for her work during which war?
questions.explain: Florence Nightingale nursed wounded soldiers during the Crimean War in the 1850s and greatly improved hygiene in military hospitals. She later founded a school for nurses in London and is regarded as the founder of modern nursing.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In which year did women in the UK gain the right to vote at the same age as men?
questions.explain: In 1918 some women over 30 were given the vote after a long campaign by suffragists and suffragettes. Ten years later, in 1928, women won the right to vote at the same age as men.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What caused the Great Famine in Ireland in the mid-1840s?
options: The failure of the potato crop
questions.explain: In the 1840s disease destroyed the potato crop on which many Irish families depended. Around a million people died and many more emigrated, especially to the United States and Britain, during the Great Famine.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which battle of 1916 saw the British army suffer its heaviest losses on a single day?
questions.explain: The Battle of the Somme began on 1 July 1916 in northern France. On the first day alone the British army suffered nearly 60,000 casualties, the worst single day in its history, and the fighting lasted for months.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who became Prime Minister in 1940 and led Britain for most of the Second World War?
questions.explain: Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in May 1940 and led the country through the Second World War. His speeches encouraged the nation at its most difficult moments, and he served as Prime Minister again from 1951 to 1955.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: On 6 June 1944, Allied forces landed on the beaches of which region to begin the liberation of western Europe?
questions.explain: On 6 June 1944, known as D-Day, British, American, Canadian and other Allied troops landed on the beaches of Normandy in northern France. It was the largest seaborne invasion in history and opened a new front against Nazi Germany.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which Scottish scientist discovered penicillin in 1928?
questions.explain: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 while working in London. Later developed by other scientists into a usable medicine, it became the first widely used antibiotic and has saved millions of lives.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: On which date is St Andrew, patron saint of Scotland, celebrated?
questions.explain: St Andrew's Day, 30 November, celebrates the patron saint of Scotland and is an official bank holiday there. The other patron saints' days are St David on 1 March, St Patrick on 17 March and St George on 23 April.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which day marks the end of the First World War and is kept as Remembrance Day?
questions.explain: The armistice that ended the First World War took effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918. Every year on Remembrance Day people remember those who died in wars, and a two-minute silence is kept at 11 am.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: On which date is Christmas Day celebrated in the UK?
questions.explain: Christmas Day, 25 December, celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ and is a public holiday across the UK. Families often exchange presents and share a special meal, traditionally including roast turkey and Christmas pudding.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the day after Christmas Day, also a public holiday, called?
questions.explain: Boxing Day, 26 December, is a public holiday in the UK. Its name is thought to come from the custom of giving boxes or gifts to servants and tradespeople, and today it is known for sporting fixtures and family visits.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What event is remembered with fireworks on Bonfire Night, 5 November?
options: The end of the Second World War
The failure of a plot to blow up Parliament in 1605
questions.explain: On 5 November 1605 a group of Catholic conspirators, including Guy Fawkes, failed in their Gunpowder Plot to blow up the Houses of Parliament and the king. People still mark the night with bonfires and fireworks.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is Hogmanay?
options: The Scottish name for New Year's Eve celebrations
questions.explain: Hogmanay is the Scottish celebration of New Year's Eve, 31 December. It is marked with parties, street events and fireworks, and in Scotland 2 January is also a bank holiday in addition to New Year's Day.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is Shrove Tuesday, the day before Lent begins, popularly called?
questions.explain: Shrove Tuesday falls on the day before Ash Wednesday, the start of Lent. It is popularly called Pancake Day because people traditionally used up rich foods such as eggs and butter by making pancakes before the Lenten fast.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: On which date is Valentine's Day celebrated?
questions.explain: Valentine's Day, 14 February, is when couples exchange cards, flowers and gifts. Some people send cards anonymously to someone they admire. It is a popular custom rather than a public holiday.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the custom on 1 April, April Fool's Day?
options: People play jokes on each other until midday
questions.explain: On 1 April people in the UK play tricks and jokes on each other, traditionally only until midday. Newspapers and broadcasters sometimes join in with invented stories, so readers need to be careful what they believe that day.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: When is Mothering Sunday celebrated in the UK?
questions.explain: Mothering Sunday falls on the fourth Sunday of Lent, three weeks before Easter Sunday. Children give cards or gifts to their mothers. Its date in the UK is different from Mother's Day in many other countries.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: On which date is Halloween celebrated?
questions.explain: Halloween, 31 October, has ancient roots in a pagan festival marking the start of winter. Today children often dress up in costumes and go 'trick or treating' to neighbours' houses, and pumpkins are carved into lanterns.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which saint's day is celebrated on 1 March?
options: St George, patron saint of England
St Patrick, patron saint of Ireland
St David, patron saint of Wales
St Andrew, patron saint of Scotland
questions.explain: St David's Day, 1 March, honours the patron saint of Wales, a sixth-century bishop. Many people wear daffodils or leeks, and schoolchildren in Wales often take part in concerts and wear traditional Welsh dress.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Wimbledon, held every summer in London, is the oldest tournament in the world in which sport?
questions.explain: The Wimbledon Championships, first held in 1877, are the oldest tennis tournament in the world. They are played on grass courts at the All England Club in south-west London and are one of the four Grand Slam events.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: 'The Ashes' is a famous series of matches between England and Australia in which sport?
questions.explain: The Ashes is a series of Test cricket matches played between England and Australia. The name comes from a mock obituary of English cricket printed after an Australian victory in 1882, and a small urn is the symbolic trophy.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: St Andrews in Scotland is known around the world as the home of which sport?
questions.explain: The modern game of golf developed in Scotland, and St Andrews is known as the home of golf. Its Old Course is one of the oldest in the world and regularly hosts The Open Championship.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Where does the sport of rugby take its name from?
options: Rugby School, a school in Warwickshire
questions.explain: Rugby takes its name from Rugby School in Warwickshire, England, where the game developed in the early nineteenth century. The two main forms today are rugby union and rugby league, both played across the UK.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: The Grand National, one of the best-known horse races in the UK, is held at which course?
questions.explain: The Grand National is a steeplechase race over high fences held each spring at Aintree, near Liverpool. Millions of people who rarely follow racing watch it or place a small bet, making it a national event.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: In 1954, Roger Bannister became the first person to do what?
options: Run a mile in under four minutes
questions.explain: On 6 May 1954 at Oxford, Roger Bannister became the first person to run a mile in under four minutes. Many had thought it impossible, and his achievement remains one of the most famous moments in British sport.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: How many times has London hosted the Summer Olympic Games?
questions.explain: London hosted the Summer Olympic Games in 1908, 1948 and 2012, more than any other city at the time of the 2012 Games. The 2012 Games also included the Paralympics, whose roots lie in the Stoke Mandeville games in England.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What are the Proms?
options: An eight-week summer season of classical concerts organised by the BBC
A series of horse races in Ascot
Formal dances held only in schools
questions.explain: The Proms are an eight-week summer season of orchestral and classical music concerts organised by the BBC. Most take place at the Royal Albert Hall in London, and the Last Night of the Proms is a famous celebration.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which city hosts the Festival Fringe, a huge arts festival held every August?
questions.explain: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe takes place every August alongside the Edinburgh International Festival. It is one of the largest arts festivals in the world, with thousands of comedy, theatre and music shows across the city.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is an Eisteddfod?
options: A Welsh festival of music, poetry and literature
questions.explain: An Eisteddfod is a Welsh festival of music, poetry and literature. The National Eisteddfod of Wales is held every year in a different location and includes competitions and performances, many of them in the Welsh language.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: The Notting Hill Carnival, a celebration of Caribbean culture, takes place in which city?
questions.explain: The Notting Hill Carnival takes place in west London every August bank holiday weekend. Started by Caribbean communities, it is one of the largest street festivals in Europe, with costumes, steel bands and food.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Who wrote the novel Pride and Prejudice?
questions.explain: Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice, published in 1813. Her novels, which also include Sense and Sensibility and Emma, describe family life and marriage among the English gentry with sharp wit and are still widely read.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which Scottish poet wrote 'Auld Lang Syne', often sung at New Year?
questions.explain: Robert Burns, the eighteenth-century poet, wrote 'Auld Lang Syne', which is sung around the world at New Year. Scots celebrate his life each year on Burns Night, 25 January, with a supper of haggis and readings of his poems.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which Victorian writer created the characters Oliver Twist and Ebenezer Scrooge?
questions.explain: Charles Dickens wrote Oliver Twist and A Christmas Carol, in which Ebenezer Scrooge appears. His novels described poverty and injustice in nineteenth-century England and remain among the most popular in English literature.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which author created the detective Sherlock Holmes?
questions.explain: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, a Scottish doctor and writer, created Sherlock Holmes, who first appeared in 1887. The detective, who lived at 221B Baker Street in London, became one of the most famous characters in fiction.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the Turner Prize, named after the painter J. M. W. Turner?
options: A prize for the best novel
An annual award for contemporary art
questions.explain: The Turner Prize is awarded each year to a British artist for an outstanding exhibition of contemporary art. It is named after J. M. W. Turner, the painter of dramatic landscapes and seascapes, and it often sparks debate.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Haggis, made from sheep's offal, oatmeal and spices, is a traditional dish of which country?
questions.explain: Haggis is a traditional Scottish dish of sheep's offal mixed with oatmeal, onion and spices. It is famously eaten on Burns Night with mashed turnips and potatoes, often called 'neeps and tatties'.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the established church in England?
questions.explain: The Church of England is the established, or state, church in England. It is a Protestant church whose spiritual leader is the Archbishop of Canterbury, while the monarch holds the title of Supreme Governor.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What kind of church is the Church of Scotland?
options: A church led by the Pope
questions.explain: The Church of Scotland is a Presbyterian church, which means it is governed by ministers and elders rather than bishops. It is the national church of Scotland, and its annual meeting is led by a Moderator elected each year.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is a pantomime?
options: A silent religious play at Easter
A comic family theatre show, usually staged around Christmas
questions.explain: Pantomimes are comic theatre shows, often based on fairy tales, performed mainly around Christmas and New Year. They include songs, slapstick and audience participation, and traditionally a man plays the role of the 'dame'.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which play by Agatha Christie is the longest-running play in the world?
questions.explain: The Mousetrap, a murder mystery by Agatha Christie, opened in London's West End in 1952 and has been performed tens of thousands of times since. It is the longest-running play in the world.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which British author created the spy character James Bond?
questions.explain: Ian Fleming created James Bond, the British secret agent known as 007, in the novel Casino Royale in 1953. The books led to one of the most successful film series ever made.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What is the National Trust?
options: A charity that preserves historic buildings, coastline and countryside
questions.explain: The National Trust is a charity founded in 1895 that looks after historic houses, gardens, coastline and countryside in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland has its own similar body, the National Trust for Scotland.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What do many people wear in the weeks before Remembrance Day as a sign of remembrance?
questions.explain: Many people wear red paper poppies in the run-up to Remembrance Day. Poppies grew on the battlefields of northern France and Belgium after the First World War, and the money raised supports former members of the armed forces.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which organisation runs the Chelsea Flower Show, held each May in London?
questions.explain: The Chelsea Flower Show is organised every May by the Royal Horticultural Society in the grounds of the Royal Hospital Chelsea. Gardening is a popular pastime in the UK, and the show displays new garden designs and plants.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which Scottish inventor gave the first public demonstration of television in the 1920s?
questions.explain: John Logie Baird, born in Helensburgh in Scotland, demonstrated television publicly in London in 1926. His early mechanical system was later replaced by electronic television, but he is remembered as a pioneer of the medium.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: Which British engineer developed the jet engine?
questions.explain: Sir Frank Whittle, an RAF officer and engineer, patented the jet engine in 1930. His work, developed in the 1930s and 1940s, transformed aviation and made modern passenger jet travel possible.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.q: What was Dolly, born in Scotland in 1996, famous for?
options: She was the oldest horse ever recorded
She was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell
She was the first animal sent into space
She was a champion racing dog
questions.explain: Dolly the sheep was born in 1996 at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh. She was the first mammal to be cloned from an adult cell, a landmark achievement in the science of genetics.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: How many members of Parliament (MPs) sit in the House of Commons?
questions.explain: The House of Commons has 650 Members of Parliament. Each MP is elected to represent one area, called a constituency, and the candidate with the most votes in that constituency wins the seat under the first-past-the-post system.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What kind of system of government does the UK have?
options: A parliamentary democracy with a constitutional monarch
questions.explain: The UK is a parliamentary democracy with a constitutional monarch as head of state. The monarch's role is largely ceremonial, while the government is formed from Parliament, which is elected by the people.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: How is the UK constitution best described?
options: It is one document written in 1215
It is the same as the US constitution
It is written in the Bible
It is not written down in a single document
questions.explain: Unlike many countries, the UK does not have a constitution set out in one single document. Its constitution is made up of laws passed by Parliament, court decisions, long-standing conventions and important historical texts.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: How do people become members of the House of Lords?
options: They are not elected by the public, mostly being appointed
They are elected every five years
They are elected by local councils
questions.explain: Members of the House of Lords are not elected by the public. Most are life peers appointed for their experience, alongside a limited number of hereditary peers and senior bishops of the Church of England.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the role of the Speaker of the House of Commons?
options: To chair debates and keep order, remaining politically neutral
questions.explain: The Speaker is an MP elected by fellow MPs to chair debates in the House of Commons. The Speaker keeps order, decides who may speak and remains politically neutral, giving up party loyalties while in the role.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the longest time that can normally pass between general elections in the UK?
questions.explain: A general election for the House of Commons must be held at least every five years. An election can take place earlier, for example if the Prime Minister asks for Parliament to be dissolved before the end of its term.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Under the first-past-the-post system, who wins a constituency in a general election?
options: The candidate with more than 75 per cent of votes
The candidate with the most votes
The candidate chosen by party members after the vote
questions.explain: UK general elections use the first-past-the-post system. In each constituency, the candidate who receives the most votes is elected as MP, even if they do not win more than half of all the votes cast.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What happens when an MP dies or resigns between general elections?
options: The seat stays empty until the next general election
The Prime Minister chooses a replacement
The House of Lords fills the seat
A by-election is held in that constituency
questions.explain: If an MP dies or resigns, a by-election is held in that constituency to choose a new MP. Only voters in that area take part, and the new MP serves until the next general election.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the Cabinet?
options: A group of senior ministers chosen by the Prime Minister
The judges of the Supreme Court
The members of the House of Lords
questions.explain: The Cabinet is made up of around twenty senior ministers selected by the Prime Minister. It meets regularly to make decisions about government policy, and its members are responsible for major departments.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Which minister is responsible for the economy and public finances?
questions.explain: The Chancellor of the Exchequer is the Cabinet minister responsible for the economy, taxation and government spending. Each year the Chancellor presents the Budget to Parliament, setting out tax and spending plans.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Which minister is responsible for crime, policing and immigration?
questions.explain: The Home Secretary leads the Home Office and is responsible for crime, policing, national security and immigration. It is one of the most senior roles in the Cabinet, often called one of the great offices of state.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the official London residence of the Prime Minister?
questions.explain: The Prime Minister's official residence and office is 10 Downing Street in central London. The Prime Minister also has a country house called Chequers in Buckinghamshire. Buckingham Palace is the monarch's London home.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the 'shadow cabinet'?
options: Senior members of the main opposition party who each follow a government area
questions.explain: The leader of the largest party not in government is the Leader of the Opposition, who appoints senior MPs to form a shadow cabinet. Each shadow minister follows the work of a government department and proposes alternative policies.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the job of party whips in Parliament?
options: To make sure their party's MPs attend and vote
To count votes at general elections
To guard the Houses of Parliament
questions.explain: Whips are MPs appointed by their parties to organise members, ensure they attend important votes and encourage them to vote with the party line. The Chief Whip often attends Cabinet meetings in the governing party.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Civil servants who carry out government policy are expected to be what?
options: Members of the House of Lords
questions.explain: Civil servants run government departments and put policy into practice. They are expected to be politically neutral and professional, serving whichever party is in government, and they are not replaced when the government changes.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: In which year did the Scottish Parliament first meet in its modern form?
questions.explain: After a referendum in 1997, the Scottish Parliament was set up and first met in 1999. Based at Holyrood in Edinburgh, it makes laws on devolved matters such as health, education and justice in Scotland.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What principle shapes the government of the Northern Ireland Assembly, set up after the 1998 Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement?
options: Government by the Republic of Ireland
Power-sharing between parties from the main communities
questions.explain: The Northern Ireland Assembly was created after the 1998 Belfast, or Good Friday, Agreement. Its government is based on power-sharing, so that parties representing the main communities share ministerial posts and decisions.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the role of the UK's constitutional monarch in government?
options: Mainly ceremonial, acting on the advice of ministers
questions.explain: The UK monarch is head of state but does not take political decisions. The monarch acts on ministers' advice, opens Parliament, gives Royal Assent to laws and meets the Prime Minister regularly, while staying politically neutral.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: At the State Opening of Parliament, who reads the speech setting out the government's plans for the coming session?
questions.explain: At the State Opening of Parliament, the monarch reads a speech in the House of Lords setting out the government's planned laws. Although the monarch delivers it, the speech is written by the government.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the Commonwealth?
options: A trading company owned by the UK
A military alliance of European countries
A voluntary association of countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire
The union of England and Scotland
questions.explain: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of independent countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire. Members work together on shared aims such as democracy, development and the rule of law, and membership is free to leave.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What position does the UK hold in the United Nations Security Council?
options: It is not a member of the UN
It holds the seat only every ten years
It is an observer without a vote
It is one of the five permanent members
questions.explain: The UK was a founding member of the United Nations in 1945 and is one of the five permanent members of the Security Council, together with China, France, Russia and the United States.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is NATO, of which the UK is a member?
options: A defence alliance of countries in Europe and North America
questions.explain: NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, is a military alliance founded in 1949. Its members in Europe and North America, including the UK, agree to help defend one another if any member is attacked.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Which organisation drew up the European Convention on Human Rights, signed by the UK in 1950?
questions.explain: The European Convention on Human Rights was drawn up by the Council of Europe, a body separate from the European Union, after the Second World War. British lawyers helped write it and the UK was among the first to sign in 1950.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Besides British citizens and eligible Commonwealth citizens, citizens of which country can vote in UK general elections if resident?
questions.explain: British citizens, citizens of the Republic of Ireland and eligible Commonwealth citizens who live in the UK can vote in general elections, provided they meet the age and registration rules and are on the electoral register.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What must you do before you can vote in a UK election?
options: Pass a citizenship test each time
Make sure your name is on the electoral register
questions.explain: To vote in the UK, an eligible person must be on the electoral register. Registering can be done online or through the local council, and voters receive a poll card telling them where their polling station is.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: During what hours are polling stations normally open on the day of a UK general election?
questions.explain: On election day, polling stations are normally open from 7 am to 10 pm, so that people can vote before or after work. Voters may also apply in advance to vote by post or by proxy.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: How many people sit on a jury in a criminal trial in England and Wales?
questions.explain: A jury in England, Wales and Northern Ireland has 12 members, chosen at random from the electoral register. Scotland uses a larger jury in criminal trials. Jurors listen to the evidence and decide whether the defendant is guilty.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Who usually hears less serious criminal cases in a magistrates' court in England and Wales?
options: Magistrates, who are usually unpaid volunteers
questions.explain: Most less serious criminal cases in England and Wales are heard in magistrates' courts. Magistrates, also called Justices of the Peace, are usually unpaid members of the local community and do not need legal qualifications.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: In England and Wales, where are serious criminal cases such as murder tried before a judge and jury?
questions.explain: Serious criminal offences in England, Wales and Northern Ireland are tried at the Crown Court, where a judge presides and a jury decides on guilt. If a defendant is found guilty, the judge decides the sentence.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: In England and Wales, which court usually hears cases against young people aged 10 to 17?
questions.explain: Young people aged 10 to 17 accused of crimes in England and Wales are usually tried in a Youth Court. The hearings are more informal, the public cannot attend, and the young person's name is not normally published.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Which court deals with civil disputes, such as unpaid debts or broken contracts, in England and Wales?
questions.explain: The County Court handles a wide range of civil disputes in England and Wales, such as debts, housing problems, contract disagreements and personal injury claims. Small claims can often be settled there without a lawyer.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the highest court of appeal in the United Kingdom?
questions.explain: The Supreme Court, created in 2009 and based in London, is the final court of appeal for civil cases across the UK and for criminal cases from England, Wales and Northern Ireland. It took over this role from the House of Lords.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Which telephone number should you call in an emergency to reach the police, fire or ambulance service?
questions.explain: In the UK, you call 999 in an emergency to reach the police, fire and rescue service, ambulance or coastguard. The European number 112 also works. Calling these numbers when there is no emergency can be an offence.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Which number do you call to contact the police when it is not an emergency?
questions.explain: The number 101 is used to contact the police in non-emergency situations, for example to report a crime that has already happened or to ask for advice. The number 999 should be kept for real emergencies.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Which organisation collects income tax and National Insurance in the UK?
questions.explain: HM Revenue and Customs, known as HMRC, collects income tax, National Insurance and other taxes. Most employees pay through the Pay As You Earn system, in which tax is deducted from wages by the employer.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What do National Insurance contributions mainly help to pay for?
options: The State Pension and certain state benefits
questions.explain: National Insurance contributions are paid by most working people and their employers. The money helps fund the State Pension and certain benefits, and the number of years of contributions affects how much State Pension a person receives.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is the minimum age for driving a car on public roads in the UK?
questions.explain: In the UK you must normally be at least 17 to drive a car on public roads. Learners need a provisional licence and must pass both a theory test and a practical driving test before they can drive alone.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: Is this statement TRUE or FALSE? It is a criminal offence to drive a car on public roads in the UK without valid insurance.
questions.explain: All drivers in the UK must have at least third-party motor insurance. Driving without insurance is a criminal offence that can lead to a fine, penalty points on the licence and even the vehicle being seized by the police.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: What is an MP's 'surgery'?
options: A private meeting of party leaders
A meeting where local people can discuss problems with their MP
An operation paid for by the state
questions.explain: Many MPs hold regular 'surgeries' in their constituency, where residents can meet them in person to raise problems or concerns. People can also contact their MP by letter, email or phone, whoever they voted for.

ref.doc: Life in the United Kingdom: A Guide for New Residents, 3rd edition (fact only, no text reproduced)
ref.section: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.chapter: The UK government, the law and your role
questions.q: In Scotland, who decides whether to prosecute people accused of crimes?
questions.explain: In Scotland, prosecutions are brought by the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service. Procurators Fiscal investigate deaths and decide whether to prosecute crimes, while most criminal cases are heard in the sheriff courts.
